question: This piece is the closing, eleventh track of an AI-generated concept album whose title insists, in its own words, that its subject remains "forever alive". It is credited to a persona called Spalexma, generally believed to be the work of songwriter Sargis Poghosyan, and appeared in more than 58,000 TikTok videos within weeks of release. Its robotic power-ballad vocals cast a slain American political commentator as a religious martyr, with a chorus vowing that its singers will "carry the flame". Posted just six days after that commentator's September 2025 assassination at a Utah college event, it debuted on Billboard's Hot Christian Songs chart, becoming one of the first believed-AI-generated songs to chart nationally. For 10 points, name this tribute song and viral solidarity phrase whose title, borrowed as a chant of unity, proclaims that its singers all share the identity of a co-founder of Turning Point USA.

A TikTok user's April 2024 post is often cited as the earliest documented use of this slang term, though a wider trend of teenagers and rappers appearing to doze mid-sentence had already circulated online since mid-2023. That year, viral clips showed people frozen in this rigid, stooped stance on sidewalks and at street corners, unknowingly filmed by passersby. The footage was widely shared to raise awareness of a powerful synthetic opioid's sedating effects, since users often exhibit this posture under its influence. More recently, some people have mimicked the pose jokingly as a dark-humor reaction gesture, unconnected to any real drug use. For 10 points, name this slumped stance, whose name plays on a shortened form of the opioid it is associated with.

Born in Ukraine in 1999, this competitive powerlifter won his weight category at the 2017 and 2018 Kyiv Cup before relocating to Dubai after Russia's 2022 invasion of his home country. His viral video format has him disguise himself as a gym janitor, secretly warming up with a mop and bucket weighing 32 kilograms each, before shocking unsuspecting gym-goers by hoisting extremely heavy barbells. In September 2026, exercise scientist Mike Israetel publicly accused him of using painted, underweight plates to fake many of his lifts. Boasting tens of millions of followers across Instagram and TikTok, he also runs a supplement brand called Arriba Nutrition. For 10 points, give this stage name of a Ukrainian strongman famous for disguised gym pranks.

The image macro version of this three-word dismissal pairs it with a 2008 panel from the comic The Incredible Hercules, in which the title character throws an enthusiastic thumbs-up at fellow hero Amadeus Cho. Know Your Meme's earliest documented use of the exact wording comes from a July 2008 thread on 4chan's video game board, aimed at a poster who had shared an overly long personal anecdote. Some trace the underlying sentiment back to a 2001 comedy in which a background character sarcastically shouts a near-identical taunt at Owen Wilson's model character. Having spread through Urban Dictionary and general forum culture by 2009, the phrase is now used to sarcastically shut down a self-important or pointless anecdote. For 10 points, give this sarcastic three-word putdown, often extended with an instruction to repeat the anecdote.

This reaction image is a black-and-white photograph of director Martin Scorsese raising both hands, taken from a January 2020 New York Times interview. It began circulating as a caption template in 2022 and 2023, building on online arguments sparked by the director's 2019 remarks dismissing certain blockbuster franchises as closer to theme parks than to serious filmmaking. Early notable posts applied the phrase to anime scenes before spreading, by April 2023, to reactions praising an NBA player's highlight performance. A related spinoff pairs the same image with an anime description ending in the phrase "kino is served", using a German loanword for a serious art film. For 10 points, give this two-word phrase of exaggerated praise, often captioned under Scorsese's raised hands to declare that something is peak filmmaking.

This term's roots trace to at least 1981, when it appeared in a dictionary of abbreviations as a blend of a word for feminine self-presentation and a term for a young man. Concentrated almost exclusively on a 4chan discussion board as of 2018, the word spread over the following years to a long-running Reddit community and then to TikTok, where a viral joke reimagining a Hooters-style restaurant staffed accordingly helped popularize it further. During 2021 pro-democracy protests in Myanmar, some demonstrators adopted feminine-coded clothing evoking this identity as a specific form of resistance against the military junta. Often associated with dyed hair, thigh-high socks, and skirts, people using this label have reclaimed what was once a near-slur into an affirming description of joyful, non-masculine gender expression. For 10 points, give this internet slang term for a boy or man who dresses and presents in a feminine style.

On January 5, 2024, hyperpop musician and streamer ericdoa was performing live on Twitch, seemingly processing grief over his grandfather's death, when he freestyled a line imagining a specific, ordinary haircut on the streamer Ninja. A clip of the moment was posted to TikTok on January 11 and quickly surpassed a million views. Just two days later, Ninja actually got that exact hairstyle in real life and posted the reveal set to the original audio, supercharging the joke's spread. The format's appeal lies in pairing sincere, emotional vocal delivery with an absurdly mundane, hyper-specific subject, and it has since been endlessly remixed by swapping in other names and hairstyles, including a parody applied to streamer Tfue. For 10 points, name this haircut, a close, gradually blended trim that became an unlikely meme after being namechecked in an emotional Twitch freestyle.

On February 27, 2025, a skincare entrepreneur going by "Veronica" accused an online critic of trying to spike a specific stress hormone in her body, sparking hundreds of thousands of views within days and a lasting catchphrase. In late 2025, TikTok creators built a simple gauge graphic, styled like a car's fuel meter running from a calm reading to an alarming maximum, to label how stressful a clip looked. That trend then merged with "looksmaxxing" online communities, which frame this hormone, believed by some to be catabolic, as something that worsens physical attractiveness and speeds aging. In January 2026, one TikToker's split-screen video comparing her own face under supposedly elevated versus reduced readings of the hormone went viral with tens of thousands of likes. For 10 points, name this stress hormone, commonly referenced in a meme phrase describing an alarmingly elevated reading on a mock stress meter.

This video pairs 1980s cartoon footage of a musclebound, sword-wielding hero's secret alter ego with an exaggerated vocal performance of 4 Non Blondes' 1992 track "What's Up?". It was first posted to the Something Awful forums in May 2005 under the title "Fabulous Secret Powers", before an unknown editor stripped out its intro and dialogue and reuploaded a tighter cut to YouTube under a nonsense string of vowels and consonants, and that stripped-down version is what actually went viral, racking up 30 million views by 2013. It inspired further mashups, including a 2006 edit setting the same cartoon footage to Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody". Today it functions as a bait-and-switch prank link, dropped into chats disguised as something else, much like a Rickroll. For 10 points, identify this early viral video built around cartoon footage of a certain 1980s toy-based hero performing vocals for a 1990s hit.

In the show's fourth season episode "Robbie's Dream Team," the villain trains his henchmen with a ska-flavored song written by Máni Svavarsson and choreographed with backup performers Björn Thors, Snorri Engilbertsson, and Bergur Þór Ingólfsson. Unnoticed for nearly two years after its 2014 airing, the song exploded in September 2016 when it was disguised as a fake Kirby Super Star Ultra track on the bait-and-switch YouTube channel SiIvaGunner. Countless remix titles followed a "but it's [gimmick]" template, popularized by figures like the DJ Grandayy and the band Radioactive Chicken Heads. When the actor who played the villain, Stefán Karl Stefánsson, announced a cancer diagnosis weeks after the song went viral, the remixing community turned its momentum into a charity fundraiser that topped one hundred thousand dollars within two months. For 10 points, name this viral earworm sung by the scheming character Robbie Rotten, proclaiming his own team's dominance.

This song comes from the show's first season, sung not by its later-famous villain but by the protagonist-side characters Stephanie, Ziggy, Stingy, and Pixel in an episode about a candy heist that first aired in North America in August 2004, a full decade before its more famous villain-sung cousin reached the internet. It built an early cult following through looping fan pages years before that later song existed, but its real breakout came in October 2008, when YouTuber HatPerson spliced in a rap verse from a 2004 Snoop Dogg collaboration credited to Lil Jon, creating the mashup most people actually recognize today. That mashup continues to circulate in TikTok and YouTube edits, and the actress who originated the character has even filmed herself reacting to it online. For 10 points, name this kids' show tune about following directions in the kitchen, remixed with a Lil Jon verse.

This exclamation comes from a mispronounced, garbled calling of a character's name in the Italian dub of a cheaply-made 2000 animated film from German studio Dingo Pictures, itself a low-budget knockoff of "The Land Before Time". In the scene, an Ankylosaurus named Peek sings a short song before an interrupting Tyrannosaurus rex named Oro shouts this exclamation at her. A clip from that Italian dub was first uploaded to YouTube in June 2010 but sat largely unnoticed for four years, before it broke out after being submitted to a Reddit community for short viral clips in August 2014, racking up over 82 million views within a few years. Fan art and photoshopped edits of the two prehistoric characters soon followed on Tumblr. For 10 points, give this nonsensical shout, now used as a general-purpose hype exclamation, torn from a poorly-dubbed European cartoon about two talking dinosaurs.

This nickname for a viral trend arose from an August 2025 caption joking that the featured types of produce depicted were "very" uncommon, ironically applied to mundane grapes, apples, and peaches. The AI-generated clips underlying the trend, made with Google's Veo 3 tool, show cartoonish produce with human-like faces eating slices of their own kind over exaggerated ASMR crunching audio. The first viral example, posted by a TikTok user in July 2025, depicted a grape eating grape slices and a kiwi eating kiwi, and later entries were also nicknamed for the unsettling, unnerving expressions on the produce's faces. The trend spread to Twitter profile picture compilations by mid-August 2025 and was covered by outlets including MSN and WikiHow as an example of absurdist low-effort content. For 10 points, give this nickname, borrowed from a word for something specialized or uncommon, for AI videos of produce cannibalizing itself.

This slang construction pairs a stress hormone's name with a 2022-origin suffix meaning that something signals a particular vibe or energy without literally being that thing, as in earlier examples describing an outfit as evoking a specific yoga-apparel brand or a personality as evoking a story's protagonist. Applied here, it describes anything, such as an outfit, a room, or a situation, as inherently stress-inducing or anxiety-triggering in feel. The underlying stress-hormone vocabulary it draws on expanded in January 2026 into online "looksmaxxing" communities, which frame the hormone as harmful to physical attractiveness and as accelerating aging. There is also an inverse, calming usage applied to soothing neutral color palettes in fashion and home decor, sometimes described as reducing this hormone's levels. Unlike a related, more literal reaction-meme phrase describing one specific triggering moment, this construction functions as a lasting descriptive label rather than an immediate reaction. For 10 points, give this slang term combining a stress hormone with a trendy suffix meaning roughly "gives off the energy of."

This Gen Alpha slang portmanteau blends a slang term for someone unattractive-looking with a German-derived word for an uncanny double. Two competing origin stories circulate: one credits a TikTok user's late-December-2025 post crediting the coinage to her best friend's boyfriend, while another says it simply arose from a mispronunciation of the word it is blended with. Its rise followed an earlier 2025 trend about a supposedly unflattering chin shape that had already pushed similar unattractive-themed slang into the mainstream. A website later emerged that uses AI to match a user's selfie to a celebrity's least flattering red carpet appearance, extending the joke into an interactive tool. Explained by one American teacher on TikTok as the discount, off-brand version of a celebrity lookalike, it can be used as a harsh insult or self-deprecatingly about a bad hair day. For 10 points, give this blended term for a less-attractive lookalike.

This catchphrase traces back to a November 2022 Facebook post in which a user recalled an old high school acquaintance's excited greeting, only to reply with a deadpan request involving ketchup instead of its now-standard condiment-free wording. That original post drew over 34,000 shares within two years, and social media users gradually swapped the condiment for a fast-food side item by early 2023. On August 16, 2023, a widely-liked post paired the line with an image of the Marvel villain Thanos. TikTok adoption came via a November 2023 video that itself racked up millions of plays, and by mid-2024 a specific skit format solidified: two former classmates reunite at a drive-through counter, one says he hasn't seen the other since school, and the unimpressed employee delivers this flat, dismissive response. For 10 points, give this deadpan retail worker's line, now used as a viral way to shut down unwanted small talk.
answer: Just put the fries in the bag, bro [or just put my fries in the bag bro]
